items.title: The Trump Comedians Are Tired
items.description: In 2017, as Donald Trump was getting used to the White House furniture, Alec Baldwin was feeling exultant. His impersonation of the new president on Saturday Night Live had made him momentarily inescapable and given the comedy show its highest ratings in years. To capitalize on the momentum, Baldwin co-authored a book-length satirical memoir written from Trump’s perspective. Baldwin’s autobiography—which also came out that year and was excerpted as a cover story for Vanity Fair —noted that his take on the president “seemed to delight nearly everyone in the People’s Republic of Manhattan.” When he accepted an Emmy for his performance in the fall, he addressed Trump directly: “At long last, Mr. President, here is your Emmy.” It was disorienting, then, to hear Baldwin declare, when I spoke with him earlier this summer, that this sort of comedy has become stale, boring, and useless. “None of it’s funny. I don’t find it funny anymore,” he told me. “There’s nothing left to say about Trump.” Clearly, something has changed—and not just for Baldwin, who effectively retired from the role back in 2020. The first Trump administration was a boon for comedians and for television. A cottage industry of new, politically inflected clip shows offered satirical commentary on the new president to a mostly liberal audience. Late-night comedy adopted Jon Stewart’s old playbook, trading quippy gags for more full-throated (and sometimes outright defiant) critiques of government. Ambiguity was out; everyone knew whose side these commentators were on, and other impersonators began vying for Baldwin’s crown. But the bubble collapsed right around the moment of Joe Biden’s ascension, and Trump’s return to power hasn’t inspired the same volume of riffs. Today, some of the comedians who rode the initial wave have come to feel a little like Baldwin does. They’re sick of the shtick—and they’re skeptical about the function of political comedy in a world that’s arguably beyond parody. [ Read: Why South Park did an about-face on mocking Trump ] Part of what once made Trump such a rich vein for comedic send-ups was that, at the start of his political career, he seemed straightforwardly ridiculous. Hadn’t this guy been shilling for Omaha Steaks with Gary Busey and Lil Jon? How would he spin the Oreo commercial he’d done with Peyton and Eli Manning, in which he’d challenged the brothers to a “lick race”? The jokes practically wrote themselves. Anthony Atamanuik, a Trump impersonator whose parody series, The President Show , ran for one season on Comedy Central in 2017, told me that at its best, the political comedy of that era also had a kind of diagnostic power: “I wanted my show to continue mostly because I saw each episode as an essay on an issue in American life, and the albatross I had was Trump.” His hope was that, for a liberal audience still reeling from the shock of his election, skewering the president could be a way to crystallize what had happened to the country. That initial burst of left-leaning satire didn’t last. Studios gave the former Daily Show correspondents Michelle Wolf, Larry Wilmore, Hasan Minhaj, and Wyatt Cenac their own shows, only to cancel them before the end of the president’s first term. A 2020 New York Times Magazine story on this “boom and bust” suggested that some comedians—and some audiences—were tiring of the material even before it became clear that Trump would lose the election. Network late-night shows continued to treat the president as a punching bag, but the novelty had worn off. Overexposure is one explanation for that decline. Another is that these liberal viewers started to expect something different from comedy as the reality of MAGA’s ascendance set in. More than over-the-top impersonators and Daily Show correspondents ridiculing the news, people seemed to be craving simple palliatives. By 2020, the most visible Trump satirist was the comedian Sarah Cooper, who filmed herself mouthing along to the president’s public statements while mimicking his facial expressions. Her work was almost post-comedic: Rather than writing her own material, she was giving people permission to laugh at the strangeness of his mannerisms. She eventually parlayed viral fame into a guest-hosting gig on Jimmy Kimmel Live and a Netflix special directed by Natasha Lyonne. Trump’s return to office in 2025 could have been an opportunity for any of these comedians to stage comebacks, or for new shows to emerge. But although the president remains a target in liberal comedy circles, the market for this brand of humor has shrunk considerably. It remains most evident in today’s late-night lineup: The Daily Show , one of the progenitors of the form, remains on the air. (Its original host, Jon Stewart, returned in 2024.) Last Week Tonight With John Oliver —which once cautioned viewers against voting for Trump by reminding them of his family’s historical surname, Drumpf—is still going too, and in a recent episode covered Trump’s efforts to reshape the Department of Justice. Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers have consistently pursued Trump since his rise; even Jimmy Fallon, who was once reluctant to get political , will now occasionally take a shot. Some new impersonators have risen to take Baldwin’s place: James Austin Johnson and Shane Gillis have both played the president with some success in recent years. But in this cohort, things aren’t quite the same as they were. Johnson’s impression hasn’t created the kind of splash that Baldwin’s once did; his version of Trump is reminiscent of the de rigueur presidential impressions of SNL seasons past. (That’s no judgment of comedic value—Johnson’s version is as accurate as it gets.) And last year, when CBS decided to end its long-running program The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , late-night TV lost one of its most prominent and consistent critics. The administration’s attempts to chill dissenting speech elsewhere, although disturbing, don’t appear to have suppressed this sort of comedy’s prevalence in American culture. And in one case, such attempts had the opposite effect: In September, ABC suspended Kimmel’s show after Federal Communications Committee Chairman Brendan Carr demanded that it do so; a few days later, in response to a public outcry, the network reversed course. The fracas turned out to be good for ratings—Kimmel’s first show back was its most-watched in more than a decade. [ Read: Jimmy Kimmel ran right at his critics ] Still, the old guard doesn’t totally see the point. “All the majors that continue to just throttle him and carry on about him—move on to other people!” Baldwin told me. “It’s not gonna make any difference.” Atamanuik told me that by fixating on Trump, comedians risk missing the bigger issues, and that young people especially have “an anger at the entire system.” (The top-three late-night talk shows have been fighting for viewers in the coveted 18–49 age demographic for more than a decade.) “They know that Trump is just a product of something else,” he said. Meanwhile, Cooper said a few years ago that she has “no desire” to revisit her lip-syncs, and that “there’s nothing left to really do with it.” Brent Terhune, another veteran of the short-form-video scene that flourished during the coronavirus pandemic, is less gloomy about the future of Trump-inflected comedy. This is partially because he’s not interested in taking on the president directly. Instead, he makes videos in the persona of a Trump fan. The character he’s played for nearly a decade, “Alpha Male,” is a sort of disgruntled MAGA vlogger—“a reaction and a reflection of people that are Trump die-hards,” Terhune told me. Part of what distinguishes the performance is that it’s at least somewhat empathetic; he said he’s always being told that Alpha Male reminds people of their brothers, dads, and uncles. His view is that because the Alpha Male character isn’t just about skewering Trump, it could potentially outlast his administration. Terhune’s enthusiasm has certainly outlasted that of many of his peers, so maybe on-screen political comedy is just in need of new subjects. Although Atamanuik no longer consistently plays Trump, he has lately been impersonating Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—and Baldwin suggested that House Speaker Mike Johnson and former Acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte could be deserving targets. Or maybe you can make the same joke only so many times before you start wondering what it is you’re really doing. In 1962, when the impressionist Vaughn Meader released his landmark comedy album, The First Family , which poked fun at the Kennedys, the anthropologist Margaret Mead remarked that its very existence illuminated something about American society. “This making fun of people in authority is very healthy,” she told Life magazine . “It is the difference between democracy and tyranny.” The impressionists I spoke with might hesitate to agree with that assessment. But beyond the easy laugh of a presidential impersonation, humor can still be a potent force in defending a free society against tyranny—that is, if comedians are willing to keep finding new angles rather than repeat old gags.

items.title: The Gun Lobby’s Most Cynical Move Yet
items.description: As a newspaper reporter, I covered my first school shooting in 2007 at Virginia Tech, where 32 students and faculty were murdered and 17 others were wounded. In one story , I recounted how Emily, a 19-year-old sophomore, was lying partially behind a desk on the floor of her French class while the shooter gunned down her teacher and nearly every student around her before shooting himself in the head. I can’t forget the image of Emily, shot twice herself, who pretended to be dead but surreptitiously grabbed a cellphone on the floor that another student had used to call 911 before he was shot. I listened many weeks later to a recording of the call. At first, she was too terrified to speak. All the police dispatcher could hear was the sound of her breath and the loud pop pop pop of gunfire all around her. “I can’t talk,” she whispered, gasping for breath. “Please hurry.” After the Virginia Tech massacre, I reported on many other school shootings, including Sandy Hook in 2012, when twenty 6- and 7-year-olds were shot to death in their first-grade classrooms and six staff members were killed. Attorney General Eric Holder, whom I covered at the time as The Washington Post ’s Justice Department reporter, told me that walking through the bullet-riddled classrooms still caked with blood was the most difficult day of his professional life. He later cried openly when he saw the crime-scene photos of the children lying dead in their classrooms. I wrote about so many school massacres that I lost count. After each one, I reached out to the National Rifle Association, the National Shooting Sports Foundation (the gun industry’s trade association), and other organizations that the nation’s gun lobby comprises for their response. They rarely commented beyond a statement offering thoughts and prayers to the victims and their families. I twice attended the world’s largest firearms trade show, held annually in Las Vegas for tens of thousands of gun makers, sellers, and other professionals but closed to the general public. There, too, leaders of the NRA, other advocates, and representatives of the multibillion-dollar gun industry would not comment on school shootings, except to reiterate their support for armed guards in schools and a government registry of mentally ill people, and to resist calls to strengthen background checks and restrict access to semi-automatic rifles such as the AR-15. [ William H. Frist: The politics of gun safety are changing. I should know. ] But the gun lobby had another response to school shootings behind the scenes—one I didn’t know about at the time. A study by Stanford University researchers this year found that after fatal school shootings, pro-gun political-action committees dramatically increased their contributions to their preferred U.S. House candidates in the districts where the shootings occurred, when those races were competitive. These shifts in spending were not observed after other incidents of mass gun violence or after nonfatal school shootings—only when children were killed in schools. Over the many years that I reported on gun violence, the gun lobby’s enormous campaign spending was no secret. But the Stanford study reveals how these groups targeted their money, raising their aggressive tactics to a new level. In the first study of its kind, the authors analyzed 25 years of data, linking campaign-finance records to every fatal K–12 school shooting from 2000 to 2024. They then compared campaign contributions between the districts that did and did not have a school shooting. After school shootings where children died, pro-gun contributions to candidates in competitive congressional districts increased on average by more than 30 percent. And when the shooting occurred within two months of an election, contributions surged by 2,820 percent. “The data shows that the gun lobby saves its political firepower for the moments when public grief is greatest and lawmakers are under the most pressure to act,” Eric A. Baldwin, one of the authors, told me. In November 2021, for example, a 15-year-old killed four students and injured seven other people at Oxford High School, in Michigan. The pro-gun PACs contributed $50,650 during the 2021–22 election cycle in the district where the high school was located, a 434 percent increase from the previous cycle and a 591 percent increase from an average of the previous five cycles, according to the Stanford researchers. In December 2013, a 17-year-old senior was killed at Arapahoe High School, in a suburb of Denver. Before the shooting, the pro-gun PAC contribution had been $1,000. Afterward, it soared to $49,470. Gun-safety PACs also increased their spending in competitive districts after school shootings. But the pro-gun groups were by far the dominant spenders until 2018, the year of the Parkland shooting, which left 17 students and faculty dead at a high school in Florida; at that point, gun-safety groups began to significantly increase their spending, sometimes equaling or even surpassing the spending of the pro-gun groups. The Stanford researchers did not find that increased spending by either side after fatal school shootings measurably affected which party actually won a competitive House election. (The districts that the study looked at represent only a subset of the gun lobby’s overall election spending.) Nevertheless, the study shows how pro-gun PACs work to undermine anti-gun feelings in communities suffering from the trauma of children being killed in schools. In poll after poll for more than a decade, the majority of Americans have favored stricter gun laws. Most Americans specifically want a ban on weapons such as AR-15s , and also favor stricter background checks. That sentiment is particularly acute after a school shooting, when “public demand for reform is especially high,” according to the Stanford researchers. But, they write, the pro-gun spending surge means that “instead of yielding to constituent pressure, candidates are fortified to resist it and are empowered to reframe their opposition to reform as principled rather than unresponsive.” [ Tyler Austin Harper: ‘How much blood is your fun worth?’ ] Although the NRA’s power has been waning in recent years, it still spent $10 million in the 2024 election. Other pro-gun groups have emerged and are influencing national policy; together with the NRA, they spend about $14 million a year on lobbying. In response to lawsuits from a number of pro-gun entities, including Gun Owners of America, a federal judge in Texas recently found unconstitutional a 1934 federal law that placed strict requirements on anyone purchasing silencers, short-barreled rifles, and shotguns, among other firearms. The Justice Department did not immediately appeal the ruling. In recent months, the Trump administration has announced new actions to make it easier for gun purchasers to avoid background checks when obtaining firearms. In April, then–Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Justice Department officials announced the rollback of gun regulations alongside leaders from the NRA, the National Shooting Sports Foundation, the National Association for Guns Rights, and Gun Owners of America. And House Republicans proposed a bill to cut nearly $300 million from the budget of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the agency that enforces the nation’s gun laws. The killing of America’s children and teenagers in their classrooms has become normalized. From a young age, our children and grandchildren are being taught vocabulary and math alongside lessons in how to hide when an “active shooter” storms their classrooms. The Stanford study is a compelling reminder of how far the gun lobby will go to block any efforts to protect our children.

items.title: Cameroun : plus de 20 décès sur »le triangle de la mort’’ en moins de deux semaines
items.description: © DR Trois accidents de la circulation dont deux graves ont ôté la vie à au moins 24 Camerounais sur les axes reliant les villes de Douala, Yaoundé et Bafoussam depuis le 14 août 2026. Plus de 20 Camerounais ont perdu la vie sur des axes routiers entre le 14 et le 23 août 2026 dans des accidents de la circulation. Le dernier remonte au 23 août 2026 sur la Nationale n° 3 (Yaoundé-Douala), à Sikoum près de Logbadjeck dans la Sanaga-Maritime. Aux environs de 6h du matin, une collision frontale entre un bus de transport en commun et un camion benne transportant du gravier fait sept morts et 10 blessés. Le drame se produit deux jours après la mort d'une autre personne au cours d'un accident de la circulation vendredi dernier à l'échangeur d'Obala. Un camion benne venant d'Obala percute le terre-plein central, projette un morceau de béton sur la voie inverse lequel renverse un véhicule de tourisme transportant cinq passagers. Cette perte en vie humaine vient augmenter le chiffre retenu une semaine avant au plus profond de l’horreur. Lors d'un autre accident de la circulation survenu à Nomale, sur l'axe Yaoundé-Bafoussam, tronçon Ndikinimeki-Bafia. 16 personnes ont rendu l'âme et une quarantaine d'autres blessées après qu'un bus a percuté de plein fouet l'arrière d'un camion chargé de bois et stationné en pleine chaussée. Tenant compte des différents événements tragiques, ce sont au total 24 morts et plus de cinquante blessés enregistrés en moins de deux semaines. Les différents accidents se produisent à une période sensible, à quelques semaines de la rentrée scolaire. Période d'intense trafic lié aux déplacements massifs des personnes entre les villes et campagnes. Entre autres causes, figurent l'excès de vitesse, le mauvais dépassement et le stationnement abusif. Un élément commun aux trois accidents est l’implication d’un camion. Pour deux sur trois des accidents, il y a implication d’un véhicule assurant le transport interurbain de personnes. Les causes vont au-delà des personnes et des véhicules et peuvent concerner les routes. Au moment où des enquêtes ouvertes sont en cours, la Fondation Camerounaise des consommateurs dénonce fermement l'insécurité routière structurelle et pointe du doigt l'état des routes. « Toutes nos routes nationales sont des voies étriquées de moins de 8 mètres de largeur, dépourvues de séparation centrale physique, où le moindre écart se transforme en choc frontal mortel », peut-on lire dans une communication du Focaco. L'organisation interpelle les pouvoirs publics en faisant remarquer que « les simples appels à la prudence ne suffisent plus » à l'approche de la rentrée scolaire et en raison de la densification du trafic. Cependant, la série de drames survient alors que le ministère des Transports mène depuis juin dernier une campagne spéciale de prévention routière. Intensifiée depuis le 17 août dernier avec l'opération d'enlèvement de véhicules mal stationnés sur les routes, ladite campagne ne semble néanmoins pas produire des résultats permettant de stopper la saignée sur les axes routiers. Des efforts et actions supplémentaires s’imposent pour mettre au point mort l’hécatombe sur les routes camerounaises. Cet article Cameroun : plus de 20 décès sur »le triangle de la mort’’ en moins de deux semaines est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Abdoulaye Maïga à Alger : plusieurs dossiers sur la table
items.description: © Internet Abdoulaye Maïga est arrivé ce lundi 24 août à Alger pour donner un contenu concret au rapprochement engagé en juillet. Sécurité frontalière, crise du Nord et échanges économiques seront au cœur des attentes. Le déplacement du Premier ministre intervient dans un climat plus favorable, mais encore chargé du contentieux récent entre les deux voisins. Invité par son homologue algérien Sifi Ghrieb, Abdoulaye Maïga doit remettre au président Abdelmadjid Tebboune un message d’Assimi Goïta. Des entretiens entre les deux chefs de gouvernement sont également prévus, selon la Primature malienne. Cette visite est la première de ce niveau depuis le retour des ambassadeurs et la réouverture des espaces aériens décidés le 10 juillet. Ces mesures ont mis fin à quinze mois de tensions provoquées par la destruction d’un drone malien près de Tinzawatène. Elles ont rétabli le contact sans régler les divergences qui avaient conduit au rappel des diplomates et à la suspension de plusieurs mécanismes de coopération. L’entretien téléphonique du 9 août entre les deux Premiers ministres avait déjà fait apparaître une volonté de renouer le dialogue. Alger affirme vouloir faire du Sahel un espace de coopération et de développement partagé. Bamako insiste, de son côté, sur la souveraineté, la non-ingérence et la prise en compte de ses intérêts sécuritaires. Frontière Le premier enjeu sera de définir une méthode de travail le long des quelque 1 400 kilomètres de frontière commune. La zone demeure traversée par les groupes armés, les trafics, les mouvements de population et des activités économiques qui échappent largement aux administrations centrales. Depuis le différend sur le drone, le Mali ne participe plus au Comité d’état-major opérationnel conjoint, installé à Tamanrasset. Cette structure associait l’Algérie, le Mali, le Niger et la Mauritanie dans le partage de renseignements et la lutte contre les menaces transfrontalières. Le retour de Bamako dans ce dispositif n’est pas annoncé. Les deux pays pourraient cependant convenir d’un nouveau cadre, plus souple, comprenant des échanges d’informations, un canal militaire permanent et un mécanisme destiné à prévenir les incidents aériens ou frontaliers. Les évolutions sécuritaires autour de Kidal donnent à la coopération avec Alger une importance particulière. À la suite des combats du 25 avril, le FLA a revendiqué la prise de la ville, tandis que les autorités maliennes ont assuré avoir maîtrisé les offensives visant plusieurs localités et poursuivi leurs opérations dans la région. Le retrait de Kidal annoncé par l’Africa Corps et le repositionnement rapporté des forces maliennes vers Anéfis ont néanmoins installé une nouvelle configuration sécuritaire à proximité de la frontière algérienne. L’organisation séparatiste a conduit son offensive parallèlement à des attaques du JNIM dans plusieurs localités du Nord. L’Algérie a depuis réaffirmé son soutien à l’unité du Mali et son rejet du terrorisme. Ce positionnement pourrait faciliter une coopération pragmatique, sans signifier le rétablissement immédiat d’une médiation politique. Bamako a dénoncé en janvier 2024 l’Accord issu du processus d’Alger, tandis que les autorités algériennes continuent de défendre une solution politique inclusive. La visite permettra surtout de savoir si les deux capitales peuvent dissocier leur coopération frontalière de leurs désaccords sur le traitement de la crise du Nord. Corridors Le rapprochement comporte aussi un volet économique important pour le Mali. La dernière Grande Commission mixte, tenue à Bamako en 2016, avait abouti à treize accords portant notamment sur l’énergie, les hydrocarbures, les mines, l’eau, la santé et le commerce. La fixation d’une nouvelle session offrirait aux deux gouvernements l’occasion de réexaminer ces engagements et de retenir quelques projets réalisables. La route transsaharienne figure parmi les dossiers les plus prometteurs. Son réseau continental est achevé à plus de 90 %, mais la liaison entre Tamanrasset, Gao et Bamako reste handicapée par l’état de certains tronçons et par l’insécurité dans le Nord. Sa mise en valeur donnerait au Mali une possibilité supplémentaire d’approvisionnement et d’accès aux infrastructures portuaires algériennes. Elle ouvrirait aussi les marchés sahéliens aux entreprises d’Algérie. Le projet de zone franche annoncé par Alger en 2024 pourrait compléter ce dispositif, à condition d’obtenir un emplacement, un calendrier et des règles de fonctionnement. Le véritable bilan de la visite dépendra donc des décisions prises après les audiences. La création de groupes techniques, la relance de la Commission mixte ou l’adoption d’un mécanisme frontalier donneraient une traduction pratique au dégel. Sans calendrier ni engagements identifiables, le déplacement restera principalement une étape politique dans une normalisation encore fragile.
